title: Partner intro: co-sell motion for regulated workloads (SI/Marketplace)
summary: Intro call with AsterBridge Consulting to explore a regulated-workloads co-sell motion (FinServ + Healthcare) around Redwood Hosted→Dedicated→Private deployments. Discussed partner fit (security-first platform modernization + data/AI programs), lead sharing + rules of engagement, how to position Redwood vs hyperscalers/LLM APIs, and a joint webinar/roundtable plan. Agreed to draft a simple co-sell intake form, align on ICP + top 25 accounts per vertical, and run a dry-run of the webinar narrative with a Redwood Private/VPC reference architecture slide.
topics:
1) Partner overview + regulated AI programs
2) Ideal customer profile and triggers (security reviews, VPC/on-prem needs, latency/cost predictability)
3) Co-sell model + account mapping
4) Lead sharing, attribution, and marketplace considerations
5) Joint webinar/roundtable: agenda, speakers, CTA, follow-up workflow
6) Next steps + owners

Markus Klein — Provide a 1-slide Private/VPC reference architecture graphic + talk track suitable for partner use (by 2026-02-06).
Soojin Lee — Share approved compliance-safe messaging snippets (retention/residency/audit logs) and “do not say” list (by 2026-02-05).
Grace O'Connor — Draft co-sell intake + lead handoff workflow (form fields, SLAs, routing) for review (by 2026-02-07).
Dana Whitmore — Send AsterBridge’s target account shortlist (top 15 FinServ + top 10 Healthcare) and indicate existing relationships (by 2026-02-10).
Noura El-Khoury — Propose 2 webinar dates + run-of-show skeleton and confirm speaker availability (by 2026-02-07).
next_steps: Schedule a 30-min working session for account mapping + rules of engagement (Redwood + AsterBridge).
Confirm webinar format (webinar vs invite-only roundtable), CTA (security review call vs architecture deep dive), and landing page ownership/UTM plan.
Align on lead-sharing expectations and what can be shared pre-NDA vs post-NDA (security artifacts, architecture diagrams).
Pick a first “design partner” opportunity to run a co-led discovery + SE deep dive within 2–3 weeks.

- For partner-sourced leads, do we require Redwood to own the contract, or can the partner lead with a services SOW + Redwood subscription (varies by customer procurement)?
- Marketplace: do we want to push AWS Marketplace private offers for FinServ first, or keep the pilot off-marketplace to reduce process overhead?
- What is the minimum security packet we can provide pre-NDA (SOC2 letter, security FAQ addendum, high-level diagram) without slowing down early stage interest?

Fireflies.ai - Transcript

Title: Partner intro: co-sell motion for regulated workloads (SI/Marketplace)
Date: 2026-02-03
Time: 3:00pm - 3:43pm PT
Duration: 43 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Camila Reyes, Markus Klein, Noura El-Khoury, Soojin Lee, Grace O'Connor
AsterBridge Consulting (SI Partner): Dana Whitmore, Ravi Iyer, Melissa Grant, Tomás Alvarez

---

[00:00] Camila Reyes: Alright, I think we’re good. Dana, Ravi, Melissa, Tomás — thanks for making time. I’m Camila, I run marketing at Redwood Inference.

[00:08] Dana Whitmore: Great to meet you, Camila. Thanks for hosting. And yeah, I’ve got Ravi and Tomás from solutions, Melissa from programs.

[00:16] Camila Reyes: Perfect. On our side, Markus is solutions engineering, Soojin is product marketing, Grace runs SDR programs, and Noura is events. The goal today is: quick intros, see if there’s an actual co-sell wedge for regulated workloads, and if yes, outline a joint webinar or roundtable and how we’d share leads without it getting messy.

[00:36] Ravi Iyer: Sounds good.

[00:38] Camila Reyes: Dana, do you want to give the thirty-second on AsterBridge and where you’re seeing demand?

[00:44] Dana Whitmore: Sure. We’re an SI focused on cloud modernization and data programs. This past, call it, 9–12 months, “GenAI” is basically in every RFP, but the regulated clients — banks, payments, providers — they get stuck. It’s less about “can it do a chatbot” and more “where does the data go, who can see it, can we audit it, can we run it in a VPC or on-prem.”

[01:08] Tomás Alvarez: And performance. Like they test something on a hosted API and it’s fine for a demo, but then procurement and risk is like, okay, show me predictable latency, show me isolation, show me logs.

[01:20] Camila Reyes: Yeah, that’s basically the thesis of why we’re doing this ABM pilot. So Redwood’s pitch in one line is: make high-performance LLM inference predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, with the same interface. The regulated wedge is Private — VPC and on-prem — plus the operational controls.

[01:40] Soojin Lee: And importantly, we try to be very precise about what is supported today vs roadmap, because security teams will ask.

[01:47] Dana Whitmore: Love that. It’s usually where folks over-promise.

[01:51] Camila Reyes: Before we go deep, Markus — can you give the “Private” framing the way you’d explain it to a platform lead?

[01:59] Markus Klein: Yeah. So, Redwood Private is essentially the Redwood control plane deployed in the customer’s environment. Usually that means their VPC — sometimes on-prem, depending. They get customer-managed networking boundaries, customer-managed keys via KMS or HSM integration points, and then we provide the inference runtime and ops tooling. There’s a shared responsibility model, like who owns patching, who owns logging pipeline, etc.

[02:26] Tomás Alvarez: When you say control plane, do you mean like the UI and the routing layer, or you deploy GPU workers too?

[02:33] Markus Klein: Both. The “runtime” — the GPU inference — runs in their environment as well. The control plane services that manage routing, policy, model versioning, those are also inside their boundary for Private. For VPC it can be peered, but the key is: no public multi-tenant endpoint by default.

[02:55] Ravi Iyer: That’s good. Most of our clients want to keep PHI or PCI-ish data from crossing into a public SaaS.

[03:03] Camila Reyes: Exactly. So the partnership idea is: you’re already in these accounts as the trusted implementer. We can show up with the platform and the security story, you bring the integration, data, governance program.

[03:17] Melissa Grant: Can I ask what verticals you’re prioritizing? Because we have two motions: financial services and healthcare, but different teams.

[03:25] Camila Reyes: For this pilot, it’s those two: FinServ and Healthcare, specifically workloads that need auditability, data residency, retention controls, and some version of private deployment.

[03:40] Dana Whitmore: Okay. That matches.

[03:42] Grace O'Connor: And from the GTM side, we’re testing messaging and outbound sequences to CISOs/GRC plus platform engineering. Partner channel could be a multiplier if we can keep the process simple.

[03:55] Dana Whitmore: Right. Simple is key.

[03:58] Camila Reyes: Let’s talk about co-sell structure. In your ideal world, what does a co-sell look like? Are you bringing us in after you find a “we need Private inference” requirement? Or do we do joint thought leadership first?

[04:14] Dana Whitmore: Both. Practically, it starts with a workshop. We do an “AI readiness / risk” workshop, then it turns into a platform selection. If we have a credible partner for private inference, we can insert you. But to generate net-new, the webinar/roundtable helps, because we can invite our CISO and platform contacts.

[04:38] Noura El-Khoury: On the webinar side, we’ve been thinking 45 minutes, with a short demo and then Q&A. For regulated folks, sometimes it’s better as an invite-only roundtable with no recording.

[04:51] Ravi Iyer: Honestly, roundtable converts better for banks. Webinar works for healthtechs.

[04:57] Melissa Grant: Also depends on if we’re allowed to use logos. Sometimes that slows everything.

[05:03] Soojin Lee: We can keep it generic, “How to deploy LLM inference for regulated workloads,” and the CTA is “architecture review.” No need to claim named customers.

[05:14] Camila Reyes: +1. We’re very careful with claims.

[05:17] Tomás Alvarez: How do you position against, say, Bedrock in a VPC? Because clients will ask, “why not just use AWS?”

[05:27] Markus Klein: Yeah. We see that question constantly. The honest answer is: if the customer is happy with the model choices and the performance/cost, and they’re okay being locked into that stack, Bedrock can be fine. Where Redwood wins is when they want more control over serving economics and operational behavior across environments — like consistent routing, fallbacks, token-level latency/cost observability, and the ability to run the same stack in VPC/on-prem without rebuilding.

[05:56] Soojin Lee: And also model lifecycle management for serving — canaries, rollback, pinning versions — plus integrations like audit log export. Those are things security teams actually care about.

[06:08] Ravi Iyer: Do you have a compliance posture? Like SOC 2, ISO, that stuff.

[06:13] Soojin Lee: Yes, and we have approved language we can share. The nuance is what we can share pre-NDA vs post-NDA. For example, we can share summary statements, but full reports under NDA.

[06:28] Dana Whitmore: That’s standard. We do the same.

[06:31] Camila Reyes: Maybe we shift into “rules of engagement” and lead sharing. Melissa, from programs, what do you need to make a co-marketing motion work?

[06:41] Melissa Grant: We need: who owns the landing page, who owns invite list, what counts as an MQL, and how leads are distributed. Also, for any joint webinar, we usually split leads 50/50 unless there’s a different agreement.

[06:56] Grace O'Connor: We can do split leads, but we also want to avoid double-spam. Our current ABM pilot is tight — 1:1-ish outreach. So I’d propose: for shared leads, we tag source, and we do a coordinated follow-up. Like one email from the partner, one from Redwood, but sequenced and with different CTAs.

[07:17] Dana Whitmore: That’s exactly what we want. If both teams blast the same person, it backfires.

[07:23] Camila Reyes: For the landing page, we can host and handle UTMs. But if your policy requires you to host, we can also supply copy and you host.

[07:34] Melissa Grant: We can do either. Hosting on your side might be faster, as long as we get reporting and lead access.

[07:41] Grace O'Connor: If it’s on our side, we route form fills into HubSpot with UTM capture. Then we can export to you daily or in real time. Also we can set up a Slack channel for hot leads.

[07:56] Dana Whitmore: That’s fine. We’ll need to make sure any lead sharing is compliant with our privacy policy. But for B2B, it’s usually okay if it’s clearly opt-in.

[08:07] Camila Reyes: Right. We’ll keep the language explicit: “By registering you agree your info is shared with Redwood and AsterBridge.”

[08:16] Tomás Alvarez: What about marketplace? Are you listed on AWS Marketplace or Azure?

[08:21] Camila Reyes: We’re in process for marketplaces, but for the ABM pilot, we’re not making marketplace the center of the story. It can add time. That said, for some FinServ procurement, AWS Marketplace private offers can speed it up.

[08:39] Ravi Iyer: Yes. Some banks like marketplace because vendor onboarding is easier.

[08:44] Markus Klein: The technical part is independent. You can still do Private deployments in their VPC. How the commercial paper flows can be separate.

[08:53] Dana Whitmore: Understood.

[08:55] Camila Reyes: Switching gears: ICP and where we think partner can help. We’re seeing triggers like: “we can’t send prompts to a public endpoint,” “we need audit logs into Splunk,” “we need retention controls,” and “we need predictable throughput.” Does that match what you see?

[09:11] Ravi Iyer: Yeah. Add “we need regional residency” — EU region, US-only. And for healthcare, BAAs come up early.

[09:21] Soojin Lee: Residency and retention is a big one. Also, we need to be careful: for Hosted, we have a defined retention posture; for Private, customer controls more. We’ll send the approved phrasing.

[09:34] Dana Whitmore: That helps. We get tripped up by vendors saying “we don’t store anything ever” and then later it’s like, well, there are logs, and security finds out.

[09:45] Markus Klein: Exactly. There are always logs. The question is what, where, and how long, and can you export and control it.

[09:54] Noura El-Khoury: For webinar content, we should probably include a “shared responsibility” slide. It’s actually reassuring.

[10:01] Camila Reyes: Agree.

[10:03] Melissa Grant: What’s the CTA you’ve seen work best? “Book a demo” is too salesy for our audience.

[10:10] Grace O'Connor: For regulated, “Security + architecture review” works better. Like: bring your platform and security lead, we’ll walk through a reference architecture and a checklist, then you decide if a POC is worth it.

[10:26] Dana Whitmore: That’s aligned with our workshop model.

[10:30] Tomás Alvarez: Can you do a performance benchmark session too? Some folks will care about latency.

[10:36] Markus Klein: Yes. We can do a “bring a sample payload” session. But we have to set expectations: we can do synthetic workloads or run in a sandbox. If they need PHI in the test, we do it only once the Private environment is set up.

[10:55] Ravi Iyer: Right, makes sense.

[10:58] Camila Reyes: Let’s outline a concrete webinar. Noura, can you propose a skeleton agenda and we can react?

[11:05] Noura El-Khoury: Sure. 1) Five minutes — “why serving is the bottleneck” in regulated. 2) Ten minutes — common architectures and where they fail: public API, self-host vLLM, hyperscaler managed. 3) Ten minutes — Redwood approach: Hosted→Dedicated→Private, with an architecture diagram. 4) Ten minutes — partner segment: “how to operationalize governance, logging, and rollout.” 5) Q&A. CTA: schedule a joint architecture + security review.

[11:38] Dana Whitmore: That’s good. I’d tweak the partner segment to be less “services pitch” and more “lessons learned.” Like top 5 pitfalls.

[11:47] Melissa Grant: And include a slide with “what you can prepare before security review” — data classification, network requirements.

[11:55] Markus Klein: That’s actually very practical. Like: do you need VPC peering, private DNS, egress allowlists, where do logs go.

[12:04] Tomás Alvarez: And identity. SSO, RBAC. People ask.

[12:09] Soojin Lee: We can include “SSO/SAML and RBAC” as a checklist item, with careful wording.

[12:15] Camila Reyes: Great. Speaker-wise: I can moderate, Markus can do technical overview, Dana or Ravi can do partner lessons, and maybe Soojin handles security messaging Q&A.

[12:28] Dana Whitmore: Ravi would be good. He’s more hands-on.

[12:31] Ravi Iyer: Happy to.

[12:33] Camila Reyes: Cool.

[12:35] Dana Whitmore: On lead list — we can invite. But we need to agree on vertical first, because our list is segmented. If we do a generic session, it becomes too broad.

[12:46] Camila Reyes: For speed, I’d propose we do one session first: “Regulated FinServ inference” and then a separate one for healthcare if it works.

[12:56] Melissa Grant: I’d vote healthcare first, actually. Healthtech founders move faster.

[13:01] Grace O'Connor: From our ABM results so far, FinServ replies are higher, but cycles are longer. Healthcare is lower volume but quicker to meetings.

[13:12] Camila Reyes: Maybe we do “regulated workloads” but tailor examples: one payments example, one PHI example. Not too specific.

[13:22] Dana Whitmore: That could work.

[13:24] Ravi Iyer: Just don’t say “HIPAA compliant” in a blanket way. That’s where it gets dicey.

[13:30] Soojin Lee: Yes. We avoid that phrasing. We talk about “supporting HIPAA-aligned controls” and “can sign BAA” only where applicable, with legal involved.

[13:42] Dana Whitmore: Great.

[13:44] Camila Reyes: Let’s talk about how we actually co-sell. Dana, do you have a standard rule — like account mapping and deal registration?

[13:52] Dana Whitmore: Yes. We typically do deal reg for partner-sourced. For co-sell, we do an account map spreadsheet: who’s in the account, who owns the relationship. Then we decide: partner-led with vendor support, or vendor-led with partner services.

[14:10] Camila Reyes: That’s workable. We’re still building partner ops, so for the pilot we can keep it simple: if you bring the lead, you’re primary; we support with SE and security. If we bring the lead and you’re a delivery partner, we can pull you in for implementation.

[14:27] Melissa Grant: And what about revenue share?

[14:30] Camila Reyes: For this pilot, we’re not trying to get fancy with rev share. We want to validate pipeline and repeatability. Long term, we can talk referral fees or services attach. But first, let’s prove the motion.

[14:46] Dana Whitmore: That’s fine. We care more about having a reliable platform partner we can bring in.

[14:52] Tomás Alvarez: Technical question: In a customer VPC, how do you handle outbound internet? Some banks block egress.

[14:59] Markus Klein: Good question. We can design for restricted egress. For model artifacts, we can support pulling from a customer-controlled registry or object store, depending on the setup. For telemetry, we can export to customer SIEM instead of sending to us. But it depends on which components they want fully isolated.

[15:22] Ravi Iyer: That’s the kind of thing we can help implement.

[15:25] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[15:27] Camila Reyes: Another partner question: what level of enablement do you need? Battlecards, pitch deck, security FAQ, that kind of stuff.

[15:35] Dana Whitmore: Yes. We need a “what to say” and “what not to say.” Also, one architecture diagram we can use in our workshops. And a simple way to get your security team on a call when we hit a hot account.

[15:50] Soojin Lee: We have the “approved phrasing vs risky claims” doc internally. We can package a partner-safe version.

[15:58] Grace O'Connor: For routing hot accounts, we can set up a shared Slack Connect channel or an email alias. Up to you.

[16:05] Dana Whitmore: Slack Connect works.

[16:08] Camila Reyes: Great.

[16:10] Melissa Grant: For the webinar landing page — do you have design resources? We can supply a logo and speaker headshots.

[16:17] Noura El-Khoury: Yes. We can do a simple landing page with both logos, speaker lineup, and a checkbox for lead sharing. We’ll also include calendar hold and reminder sequence.

[16:31] Ravi Iyer: How do you handle follow-up? Like do you have a playbook?

[16:35] Grace O'Connor: Yes. We do a 3-touch sequence: (1) resource recap + link to reference architecture and security FAQ, (2) invite to architecture review, (3) performance benchmark offer. But we coordinate with partner so it doesn’t overlap.

[16:54] Dana Whitmore: Perfect.

[16:56] Camila Reyes: Quick check: any red flags, or does this feel like a fit?

[17:01] Dana Whitmore: Fit. The only thing is we need clarity on what’s real in Private today, like what’s GA vs beta.

[17:09] Soojin Lee: Totally fair. We’ll provide that, and we’ll flag anything that’s roadmap-sensitive.

[17:16] Tomás Alvarez: Another question: do you support on-prem in a fully air-gapped environment?

[17:22] Markus Klein: We have an on-prem package, but air-gapped specifics depend on constraints — like how updates and model artifacts get in. For the webinar, I’d keep it to “VPC and on-prem options,” and for any specific air-gap requirements, we’d do a separate technical deep dive.

[17:41] Ravi Iyer: Makes sense.

[17:43] Camila Reyes: Alright. If we’re aligned, I’d like to close with concrete next steps and owners.

[17:48] Dana Whitmore: Yep.

[17:50] Camila Reyes: From Redwood: I’ll send a partner overview one-pager. Markus will send a slide version of the Private/VPC reference architecture. Soojin will send messaging snippets, including retention/residency and audit log phrasing. Grace will draft the co-sell intake and lead handoff workflow. Noura will propose two webinar dates and a run-of-show.

[18:17] Melissa Grant: Great.

[18:18] Camila Reyes: From AsterBridge: Dana, can you send a shortlist of target accounts — even 20–25 — split FinServ/Healthcare, and note where you have relationships?

[18:29] Dana Whitmore: Yes. I can do that next week. Probably by Tuesday.

[18:34] Camila Reyes: Perfect.

[18:36] Ravi Iyer: And I’ll work with Melissa on suggested talk track for the “pitfalls” section.

[18:42] Noura El-Khoury: Awesome.

[18:43] Camila Reyes: One more operational thing: do we need an NDA before we share anything? We can keep initial materials high level.

[18:52] Dana Whitmore: For high level, no. If you’re sharing SOC2 report, yes.

[18:57] Soojin Lee: We won’t share full reports without NDA.

[19:00] Camila Reyes: Great.

[19:02] Dana Whitmore: This is good. Appreciate how direct this is.

[19:05] Camila Reyes: Same. Okay, we’ll follow up by email with the recap. Thanks all.

[19:11] (crosstalk)

[19:12] Melissa Grant: Thanks.

[19:13] Ravi Iyer: Thanks everyone.

[19:15] Tomás Alvarez: Thanks.

[19:16] Camila Reyes: Bye.

---

Note: Transcript ends early due to Fireflies export trimming; remaining time was small talk and calendar scheduling.
